A long distance trade in mules, bred on the plains of what is now Argentina and driven north to the mines and roads of Peru and the Andes. By 1776 Peru was using about half a million mules, many of them raised half wild on the pampas.

Before engines, animals did nearly all the hauling. In the steep Andes, mules were better than horses or llamas: strong, sure-footed and able to carry heavy loads on narrow trails. They moved the silver of Potosí, mercury, wine, cloth and food between the mines, the cities and the coast.

Each year tens of thousands of young mules were driven from the pastures of the Río de la Plata through Córdoba to Salta, where a great mule fair was held, and then on into the highlands. The trade tied the grasslands of the south to the silver economy of the Andes, and gave the cattle country of the gauchos a market long before it sold beef to Europe.
